1212.title: Tuladhara's honest scale
1212.hook: a great ascetic is sent to a market stall to learn dharma
1212.carry: dharma lives at an honest counter too
1212.howItsDone: Hindu teachers sometimes retell the dialogue of Tuladhara and Jajali from the Mahabharata to show that honest work in an ordinary trade can itself be a way of dharma.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Yudhishthira's great sacrifice, Krishna washed the guests' feet: in seva, God takes the job at the feet.
screen: `KRISHNA WASHES THE GUESTS' FEET.` · `GOD TAKES THE JOB AT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: A man stands in the forest so still, for so long, that a pair of birds builds a nest in his matted hair. That's how the Mahabharata tells it. His name is Jajali, an ascetic. The birds lay their eggs. The eggs hatch. He stays still until the chicks grow wings, fly off, and stop coming back. Then a thought arrives, and it's a proud one: who in the world is my equal in dharma? An unseen voice answers. Not you, Jajali. There's a merchant in Varanasi named Tuladhara, and you are not his equal.
screen: `BIRDS NEST IN HIS HAIR.` → `WHO IS MY EQUAL?` → `A MERCHANT IN VARANASI.`

segments.voice: So Jajali goes to Varanasi and finds him, a trader selling goods in the market. Before Jajali can say a word, Tuladhara greets him and tells him his own story: the stillness, the birds, the proud thought, the voice. Jajali asks how a trader could know this. Tuladhara's answer, in paraphrase, is the teaching. He knows the ancient dharma, he says, and he names it plainly: friendship toward all beings, and a way of living that harms them as little as it can. He earns his bread by trade, and keeps it honest. He doesn't cheat on the weight. He doesn't flatter or run anyone down to make a sale. He holds the same even scale for everyone who comes to his counter. Even his name fits. In Sanskrit, a tula is a balance, and Tuladhara can be heard as the one who holds the scales. In this story, the scale on the counter and the evenness in his mind are one practice. Now notice who's teaching whom. The great ascetic walks all the way to a market to learn from a man who weighs things for a living. The Mahabharata doesn't tell Jajali to open a shop, or call his years in the forest a waste. It says dharma was already sitting at that counter, in an honest weight handed to a customer Tuladhara might never see again. That's the teaching: dharma isn't only for forests and temples. Honest work, done without harm, can itself be dharma and seva.
screen: `TULADHARA TELLS JAJALI HIS OWN STORY.` · `FRIENDSHIP TOWARD ALL BEINGS.` · `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SCALES.` · `DHARMA AT THE SHOP COUNTER.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands palm up on your knees, like the two pans of a balance, and bring to mind one exchange waiting for you: a sale, a report, a favor, a reply. Notice where you'd be tempted to tip it a little, a corner cut, a bit of flattery, then let both hands rest evenly again and breathe there. If you pray, you can offer that exchange to God as it is.
Seva as vocation. Service done through the work itself, the way Tuladhara served everyone who trusted his scales.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: dharma lives at an honest counter too. A scale held level serves every buyer who trusts it, whether or not anyone notices. See you tomorrow.

1213.title: The renouncer who keeps working
1213.hook: Arjuna asks which is better, quitting or working, and Krishna redraws the renouncer
1213.carry: karma yoga: drop the fruit, not the work
1213.howItsDone: Hindu teachers of karma yoga turn to the opening of the Gita's sixth chapter to explain that renunciation can be practiced inwardly, by letting go of the fruit of action while continuing to work.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: dharma lives at an honest counter too. At his market stall, Tuladhara held the same even scale for everyone, and taught an ascetic with birds in his hair.
screen: `TULADHARA'S LEVEL SCALE.`

segments.voice: On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna has already said he'd rather live on a beggar's alms than fight. Krishna has praised both letting go and action, and Arjuna is confused. At the start of chapter five he asks: you praise giving up action, and you praise the yoga of action. Tell me for certain which one is better. Krishna's answer: both lead to the highest, but of the two, the yoga of action is better. Hindu tradition honors the sannyasi, the renouncer who gives up home, possessions and the household fire. And a chapter later, Krishna redraws who counts as one.
screen: `ARJUNA: I'D RATHER BEG.` → `WHICH IS BETTER?` → `THE YOGA OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse that opens chapter six, in paraphrase. The one who does the work that ought to be done, without leaning on its fruit, is a renouncer, and a yogi. Not the one who has merely put out the fire. Not the one who has merely stopped acting. Take it in pieces. The work that ought to be done: in Sanskrit, karyam karma. The work that's actually yours to do, today. Without leaning on its fruit: the word is anashritah, not taking shelter in, not propping yourself up on. The fruit is the result: the praise, the raise, the thank-you. The verse doesn't say results don't matter. It says don't lean your whole weight on them. And the fire: commentators read it as the household's sacred fires, which a renouncer no longer tends. Putting out the fire doesn't make you free; letting go inwardly does. The next verse makes it plain: what people call renunciation, Krishna says, know that to be yoga. This is karma yoga, the path of action, one of the great paths of Hinduism: your own work, offered, without clinging to its fruit. Yesterday a merchant held his scale level in a crowded market. Today Krishna tells a warrior the deepest letting go can happen without leaving the field. Read this way, the Gita leaves room for a nurse, a farmer or a clerk to renounce too, without leaving the work.
screen: `THE WORK THAT OUGHT TO BE DONE.` · `NOT LEANING ON THE FRUIT.` · `PUTTING OUT THE FIRE ISN'T THE THING.` · `KARMA YOGA: A RENOUNCER WHO KEEPS WORKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one piece of work waiting for you and notice the fruit you're leaning on, the reply, the approval, the result, and where that leaning lives in the body, maybe the shoulders, maybe the jaw. On each out-breath, shift your weight back onto your own two feet: the work is still there and you still care how it goes, you're just not hanging on it. If you pray, you can offer the result to God and keep the work.
Seva as vocation. In the Gita's sixth chapter, the renouncer is the one who does the work that's theirs, without leaning on its fruit.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma yoga: drop the fruit, not the work. The renouncer isn't defined by the robe or the cabin. Back tomorrow, same hill.

screen: `DAY 1213 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOVE IS THE FRUIT.`

1214.title: Love is the fruit
1214.hook: Narada brags, gets a monkey's face, and his sutras say love is the fruit
1214.carry: bhakti is the fruit, and God loves humility
1214.howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied in short sections with a teacher, and lines like these on love as the fruit and the Lord's fondness for humility are explained with stories of devotees.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: karma yoga, drop the fruit, not the work. The Gita's renouncer never quits the job, but stops leaning on the fruit.
screen: `DROP THE FRUIT, NOT THE WORK.` · `THE RENOUNCER KEEPS WORKING.`

segments.voice: You may remember the sage Narada from year one. He sat so deep in meditation that Kama, the god of desire, couldn't move him, and Narada was thrilled with himself. He bragged to Shiva, then to Vishnu. Then, in a city Vishnu conjured, he fell for a princess and begged Vishnu for his handsome face so she'd choose him. He walked into her hall with the face of a monkey. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it. Tradition credits that same Narada with a short book on love, the Narada Bhakti Sutras. Today it makes its boldest claim, with a reason the monkey-faced Narada would understand.
screen: `NARADA BEATS DESIRE.` → `AND BRAGS ABOUT IT.` → `A MONKEY'S FACE.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: bhakti, the sutras say, is greater even than karma, jnana and yoga: action, knowledge and the disciplined stilling of the mind. Why? Because it is of the form of the fruit. Phala-rupa. The fruit is what the tree is for. So the sutras aren't calling the other roads worthless. They're saying love is what those roads walk toward: work done as an offering, knowing that clears the mind, a mind held still, all finding their point in love. Then a second reason. The Lord, the sutras say, dislikes pride and is fond of humility. The Sanskrit for that humility is dainya: lowliness, the state of someone with empty hands. Narada had beaten desire and turned the win into a trophy, and the princess's hall took it from him. In the sutras' picture, love has a hard time doing that, because it keeps looking at the beloved, not at itself. That's the heart of bhakti, the path of loving devotion that runs through so much Hindu worship: the bhajan, the lamp, the flower offered with folded hands are meant as gifts, not performances. That's this text's view; other Hindu teachers weigh the roads differently. Shankara's school, which we met in year two, holds that knowledge is what frees, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Both are living Hindu paths. Tomorrow the sutras ask, out loud, whether knowledge is the means to love.
screen: `PHALA-RUPA: LOVE IS THE FRUIT.` · `THE LORD LOVES HUMILITY.` · `GIFTS, NOT PERFORMANCES.` · `SHANKARA: KNOWLEDGE FREES.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and notice anything you're holding up like a trophy today: something you did well, something you know, how long you've practiced. Don't scold it; set it down beside you the way you'd put down a bag, and rest with the hands open. If you pray, you can turn toward God with those open hands; if not, simply stay with what it's like to hold nothing up.
Bhakti. In the Narada Bhakti Sutras, not only a road but the fruit itself, and close to humility, dainya, the open hand.
screen: `BHAKTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti is the fruit, and God loves humility. Offer it as a gift, not a trophy. Until tomorrow.

1215.title: The king and the meal
1215.hook: Narada knew every Veda and was still hungry; the sutras answer with a king and a meal
1215.carry: bhakti is lived, not just known
1215.howItsDone: Teachers of the Narada Bhakti Sutras use the king and the meal to explain that devotion is something lived, not only studied, and pair the study of the text with worship, singing and service.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: love is the fruit, not only the road, and the Lord is fond of humility, empty hands.
screen: `LOVE IS THE FRUIT.` · `EMPTY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Year two met Narada in the Chandogya Upanishad, sitting before the sage Sanatkumara with a whole library in his head: all four Vedas, the old stories, grammar, mathematics, the stars. Then he said the honest sentence. Sir, I know the sacred texts, but I do not know the Self. And I am in sorrow. Take me across. Hold on to that scene, because today the Narada Bhakti Sutras ask the same question about love. If love is above the other roads, how do you get it? Isn't knowledge the way in?
screen: `NARADA KNOWS EVERYTHING.` → `AND IS STILL IN SORROW.` → `ISN'T KNOWLEDGE THE WAY IN?`

segments.voice: The sutras answer the way they did on the marks of love in year two: they let several voices speak. Some say, the text reports, that knowledge alone is the means to bhakti: you have to know who the Lord is before you can love him. Others say knowledge and love depend on each other: picture two cards propped into a little tent. Then a third voice, the sons of Brahma, whom commentators take to be Sanatkumara and his brothers, the ever-young sages of the Puranas. Sanatkumara: the same teacher who heard Narada admit his learning hadn't freed him. They say bhakti is its own fruit, not produced by something else. Here the sutras side with them, and give their evidence: a king, a house, and a meal. Knowing about a king doesn't make the king pleased with you. Knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger. So, the sutras conclude, those who long for freedom should take up love itself. Notice what they don't say. Not that knowledge is bad, or that you should stop learning. Narada was a great scholar. The sutras just refuse to let knowing about stand in for the thing. That's why devotional Hindus don't stop at reading. They sing the names, offer the lamp, stand for darshan, take prasad. The scripture tells you about the meal; worship is where you eat. The king has to be met. The meal has to be eaten.
screen: `SOME SAY: KNOWLEDGE IS THE MEANS.` · `THE SONS OF BRAHMA: ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `THE KING AND THE MEAL.` · `WORSHIP IS WHERE YOU EAT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you love and notice, for a few breaths, how much you know about them: their habits, their history, the facts. Then let the facts go quiet and simply be near them, the way you'd sit beside someone without needing to talk. If you pray, you can do this with God, setting aside what you know about God for a while.
Bhakti. For the sutras, its own fruit: knowing about the king doesn't please him, and knowing about the meal doesn't feed you.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti is lived, not just known. Knowing about the meal isn't eating it. See you tomorrow.

1216.title: The company of great souls
1216.hook: a servant's boy among singing sages, and the sutras' chief means of love
1216.carry: love of God is caught in satsang
1216.howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, people gather for satsang, sitting with teachers and fellow devotees to hear and sing about God, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras' lines on the company of great souls are a familiar reason given for it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the king and the meal: knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger, and love is its own fruit.
screen: `THE KING AND THE MEAL.` · `ITS OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, Narada tells how he began. In an earlier life, he says, he was the small son of a maidservant. One rainy season a group of sages came to stay where his mother worked, and the boy was set to serve them. He fetched water, kept quiet, ate what they left with their permission, and every day heard them singing and telling the stories of Krishna. No study, no vow. And a taste for Krishna woke up in him, growing with every hearing. Today the sutras credited to that same Narada list how love begins, and name the one means they call chief.
screen: `A SERVANT'S BOY.` → `ONE RAINY SEASON WITH THE SAGES.` → `LOVE WAKES UP.`

segments.voice: The teachers sing of its means, the sutras say, and list them. Letting go of the pull of sense objects, and of clinging attachment. Worship that doesn't break off. Hearing and singing the qualities of the Lord, even while living an ordinary life in the world. So the means aren't only for a monastery. Then the sutras turn. But chiefly, love comes by the grace of great souls, or by a drop of the Lord's own grace. After the list of things a person can do, the main source is something given. Then three phrases about the company of the great, mahat-sanga. It is hard to find. It is hard to fathom. And in the sutras' view, it never fails. Then a line that holds the section together. Between him and his people, there is no difference. To be near those who love God, in this text, is already to be near God. And the section ends with a sentence said twice, like a teacher tapping the table: strive for that alone, strive for that alone. Narada's own beginning is this teaching lived out. It's why Hindus prize satsang, the company of the true: the bhajan circle, the temple hall, a grandmother who brings you along. In the sutras' picture, love of God travels from those who have it to whoever sits near.

1217.title: Ripples become an ocean
1217.hook: one glimpse swallows Ajamila's life; the sutras on ripples and who crosses
1217.carry: dussanga turns ripples into an ocean
1217.tomorrow: A taste that can't be told
1217.howItsDone: Devotional teachers explain the sutras on bad company as advice to guard the mind, and pair it with the positive practice of satsang, keeping company that nourishes love of God.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the company of great souls: hard to find, hard to fathom, never failing, and no difference between the Lord and his people.
screen: `THE COMPANY OF GREAT SOULS.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, Ajamila is a young Brahmin with a good name: learned, gentle, careful in his duties. One day his father sends him to the forest for flowers and kindling. On the way home he sees a man and a woman of the town, drunk and laughing in each other's arms. It's one glimpse. He tries to steady his mind with all he's studied, and can't. He keeps thinking of her, keeps going back, and the thought is fed until it swallows everything: his father's wealth, his young wife, his good name. Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras give that a picture: ripples becoming an ocean.
screen: `ONE GLIMPSE ON THE ROAD.` → `FED, DAY AFTER DAY.` → `IT SWALLOWS A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bad company, dussanga, is to be given up in every way, the sutras say. And they give the reason as a chain. It causes desire, then anger, then delusion, then the loss of memory, then the loss of understanding, and then the loss of everything. Then the image: though these arise only like ripples, through company they become an ocean. A flash of desire or anger isn't a disaster in itself. A ripple is a ripple. What turns it into an ocean is company: whatever keeps feeding it, a person, a place, a feed on a screen. Many teachers read Ajamila's fall exactly this way: one glimpse, fed day after day. Then a question, asked twice: who crosses? Who crosses over maya, the great illusion? The answers come in short lines. The one who gives up clinging, serves the great, becomes free of mine, goes beyond the pairs of opposites, like pleasure and pain, and comes to a love that doesn't break off. That one crosses, that one crosses, and helps the worlds cross too. And Ajamila? You met his ending in earlier years: old and afraid of death, he called his son's name, Narayana, and Vishnu's messengers came. The Bhagavata says he then went to Haridwar on the Ganga and gave his last years to devotion. Even the man the ocean swallowed got across. That's why Hindu families guard their company and seek out satsang: in this teaching, the mind takes the shape of what it keeps near.
screen: `DUSSANGA: A CHAIN OF LOSSES.` · `RIPPLES BECOME AN OCEAN.` · `WHO CROSSES? WHO CROSSES?` · `EVEN AJAMILA CROSSED.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later something will rise, an irritation, a wanting, a worry; notice it the way you'd notice a ripple on water. Don't push it down and don't feed it, no replaying the argument, no adding the next thought; just watch it rise and flatten out on its own. If you pray, you can hand each ripple to God as it passes.
Bhakti. In the sutras, it's guarded from the company that turns ripples into an ocean, and it carries those who cross.

1218.title: A taste that can't be told
1218.hook: Dhruva can't find a word before Vishnu; the sutras on a love that can't be told
1218.carry: bhakti can't be told, only tasted
1218.howItsDone: Devotional teachers quote the sutras' image of a taste that a person who cannot speak cannot describe, to explain why bhakti is passed on through singing, stories and company rather than argument.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti and the ripples: through company they become an ocean, and the one who crosses helps the worlds cross too.
screen: `RIPPLES BECOME AN OCEAN.` · `WHO CROSSES?`

segments.voice: Year one met Dhruva, the five-year-old prince pushed off his father's lap, who went into the forest and held Vishnu in his heart for months. Then the inner vision vanished, he opened his eyes, and Vishnu was standing in front of him. The Bhagavata says the boy gazed as if drinking him in. He longed to praise him, and couldn't find a single word, until Vishnu touched his cheek with the conch and the praise poured out. Hold that boy in mind: full to the brim, and speechless. Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras try to say what love itself is like, and they start by admitting they can't.
screen: `DHRUVA OPENS HIS EYES.` → `NO WORDS.` → `WHAT IS LOVE ITSELF LIKE?`

segments.voice: The nature of love, the sutras say, cannot be told. Anirvacaniya. Then the comparison: it's like the tasting of someone who cannot speak. The taste is completely real; it just can't get out in words. It shows itself in a vessel fit for it: not everywhere at once, not on command, but in a particular person, at a particular time, the way it filled a small boy in a forest. Then the sutras try anyway, with a string of qualities. It is free of the qualities that color ordinary feeling. It is free of wanting something back. It grows every moment. It doesn't break off. It is subtler than the subtle. And it is a matter of experience, not of theory. The things we like wear down with use. The sutras say this love does the opposite: the longer it runs, the more of it there is. And someone who has it? Having gained it, they see only that, hear only that, speak only of that, think only of that. That's why bhakti in Hinduism is handed on by singing, stories and company more than by argument: you can't explain a taste, but you can share the plate. Look back at the week: Tuladhara's honest scale, the renouncer who keeps working, Narada's monkey face, Narada in sorrow before Sanatkumara, Narada the servant boy among singers, Ajamila's ripple, and a boy struck speechless. Tomorrow, the last pages: the people who have this love.
screen: `ANIRVACANIYA: IT CANNOT BE TOLD.` · `GROWING EVERY MOMENT.` · `SEE ONLY THAT, HEAR ONLY THAT.` · `YOU CAN SHARE THE PLATE.`

segments.voice: Bring back a moment when you were deeply happy with someone or something you love: the light, the sound, the feeling in the chest. Each time a word tries to describe it, let the word go and go back to the taste, no commentary, no captions. If you pray, you can rest in God the same way, without words.
Bhakti. In the sutras, a love that can't be told, like a taste for someone who cannot speak, and it grows every moment.
